t: Count Subarrays With Median K — Prefix Sum on Balance Values
o: We must count contiguous subarrays whose median equals k. Since the array is a permutation of 1..n, every element is either less than k, greater than k, or equal to k itself. A subarray has median k exactly when it contains k and the number of elements greater than k never exceeds the number of elements less than k by more than... more precisely: for odd length 2m+1 the median is k iff (#greater - #less) = 0; for even length 2m+2 the median (left middle) is k iff (#greater - #less) = 1. In Example 1 (nums = [3,2,1,4,5], k = 4): subarray [4] works trivially; [4,5] has one greater element and zero smaller ones, so median of length-2 array is the left middle = 4; [1,4,5] has one smaller and one greater, median 4. In Example 2 ([2,3,1], k=3), only [3] qualifies since [3,1] has median 1 and [2,3] has median 2. The n up to 1e5 constraint rules out enumerating all subarrays naively in the worst case beyond an O(n^2)-style scan, pushing us toward a linear prefix-sum/hash-map solution.
k: A subarray containing k has median k iff (#elements > k) - (#elements < k) is 0 (odd length) or 1 (even length).
Split at position of k: count balance values to the left with a hash map, then sweep right accumulating balances.
Map each element to +1 if > k, -1 if < k; the running sum around k is the balance.

a.i: For each starting index i where nums[i] == k we could expand outward, but simplest correct version: for every pair (i, j), check whether the subarray contains k and its sorted left-middle element is k. Checking requires sorting or counting per subarray. We can speed the check slightly by counting how many elements are greater/less than k while extending j, but the pure brute force sorts each candidate. This is only feasible for small inputs but establishes correctness of the median condition.
s: For each start i, iterate end j from i to n-1.
Collect nums[i..j], sort it, compute the left-middle index (len-1)/2.
If that element equals k, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n^3 log n) worst case — O(n^2) subarrays, each sorted in O(n log n); far too slow for n = 1e5 but fine conceptually.
a.sp: O(n) for the temporary copy of the current subarray.

a.n: Approach 2: Prefix Balance Counts with Hash Map (Optimal)
a.i: Only subarrays containing k matter. Map values to +1 (>k), -1 (<k). Let pos be the index of k. For a subarray [l, r] with l <= pos <= r, define bal(l, r) = (#greater) - (#less). The median is k iff bal = 0 (odd length) or bal = 1 (even length). Sweep r from pos rightward maintaining suffix balance sb(r) = bal(pos, r). Then bal(l, r) = sb(r) - pre(l), where pre(l) = bal(l, pos-1) computed over indices l..pos-1. Store counts of each pre value seen so far in a hash map; for each r add map[sb(r)] + map[sb(r) - 1]. Initialize map[0] = 1 to account for subarrays starting exactly at pos.
s: Find index pos of k; build map from values: +1 if > k else -1.
Walk left from pos-1 to 0 accumulating balance pre; store counts of pre in hash map, seeding map[0] = 1.
Reset balance to 0 and walk right from pos to n-1 accumulating balance sb.
For each r, add map[sb] (odd-length case) plus map[sb - 1] (even-length case) to the answer.
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes over the array with O(1) amortized hash map operations.
a.sp: O(n) — the hash map can hold up to n distinct left-prefix balance values.

w: In an interview, go straight to Approach 2 after stating the key observation about the balance condition; mention brute force only briefly to justify the transition. Common pitfalls: forgetting the even-length case (bal = 1, i.e., counting map[sb - 1]), forgetting to seed map[0] = 1 for subarrays starting at pos, and misdefining the direction of the sign (+1 for greater vs. less — both work as long as consistent, since conditions become symmetric). Edge cases: k at index 0 or n-1 (one side contributes nothing), n = 1 (answer is 1). Follow-ups: what if elements were not distinct (handle ties carefully), or if you needed the count for every k (would require a different technique like divide and conquer).
